note: M1. Core fork: Shannon information (syntactic/bits/brute force) vs Simon information (semantic/lists/modularity). Reference entities (credit assignment, reinforcement learning, society of mind, combinatorial explosion, temporal differencing) are re-declared minimally so cross-session relations resolve and the source link is recorded; their definitions were set in session 1.

entities.name: information processing
entities.definition: Any use of information (storing, manipulating, displaying, trafficking in symbols) by agents interacting with a problem-solving environment to learn to assign credit; the session's reframing of credit assignment as message passing among agents.

entities.name: Shannon information
entities.definition: Claude Shannon's approach: information is syntactic, its unit is the meaningless bit, and intelligence is ultimately a matter of brute force (channel capacity).

entities.name: Simon information
entities.definition: Herbert Simon's approach: information is semantic, its unit is the meaningful list, and intelligence is a matter of abstracting/modularizing a problem rather than adding capacity.

entities.name: bit
entities.definition: A meaningless binary digit (0/1); the building-block unit of Shannon information, linked into bit strings that encode any symbol.

entities.name: list
entities.definition: A named, meaningful unit (a label that designates objects/concepts in the world, followed by items) that can be linked into arbitrarily abstract structures; Simon's building-block unit.

entities.name: brute force
entities.definition: Assigning credit by pairing an embarrassingly simple strategy (e.g. a value function) with massive channel capacity; the strategy Sutton's 'bitter lesson' celebrates.

entities.name: modularity
entities.definition: Assigning credit by abstracting a problem into meaningful modules (Simon's watchmaker), so the agent processes higher-level lists rather than every detail.

entities.name: physical symbol system hypothesis
entities.definition: Newell & Simon's hypothesis that physical symbols (symbols meaningfully referring to the world, not just stored bit strings) are a necessary and sufficient basis for intelligence.

entities.name: watchmaker parable
entities.definition: Simon's parable (Architecture of Complexity, 1962): a watchmaker who decomposes a 1,000-part watch into named modules finishes vastly faster under interruption than one assembling part-by-part — the case for modularity.

entities.name: Claude Shannon
entities.definition: MIT co-founder of the field; introduced information theory, bits, and entropy, and built the maze-learning robot Theseus (1950).

entities.name: Herbert Simon
entities.definition: Carnegie-Mellon co-founder of the field; proposed semantic/list-based information, the physical symbol system hypothesis (with Newell), satisficing, and modular decomposition.

relations.evidence: Shannon information is Approach 1 to information processing.
Simon information is Approach 2 to information processing.
Assigning credit is reframed as an information process of evaluating patterns in symbols.
Shannon proposed bits as the building-block units of syntactic information processing.
Simon proposed lists as the units of meaningful information.
Shannon information implies credit assignment is ultimately a matter of brute force (channel capacity).
Simon information implies credit assignment through modular abstraction.
Shannon's claim: a linear increase in channel capacity can exponentially reduce signal-to-noise, offsetting combinatorial explosion.
Modular decomposition lets an agent describe a problem with fewer, higher-level lists.
Sutton's value function is the 'embarrassingly simple strategy' paired with scale in the bitter lesson.
Simon's watchmaker parable illustrates the gains of modular decomposition under interruption.
Newell & Simon's Turing Award articulation of list processing.
Physical symbols are claimed necessary and sufficient for intelligence (efficient credit assignment).

claims.proposition: Assigning credit is an information process of evaluating (matching or recognizing) patterns in symbols about problems; AI ideas differ in which symbolic patterns they take as the basic unit of information.
Under Shannon information, the unit is the meaningless bit and an agent's ability to assign credit is entirely a matter of capacity for processing syntactic information over a limited channel.

The brute-force assumption is that any combinatorial explosion in problem complexity will be more than offset by the exponential increase in signal-to-noise from a linear increase in channel capacity.
claims.conditions: holds if added channel capacity compensates for combinatorial complexity

claims.proposition: Under Simon information, the unit is the meaningful list that designates objects in the world, and intelligence comes from finding better, higher-level abstractions rather than adding channel capacity.

The modularity assumption is that adding bigger computers will NOT produce a disproportionate increase in a system's ability to assign credit; one is better off decomposing the problem into meaningful modules.
claims.conditions: holds when better abstractions, not capacity, are the binding constraint

claims.proposition: Shannon information assumes outcomes are independently and identically distributed (IID) — the world stays the same — whereas real-world credit assignment is often out-of-distribution (OOD), which was Minsky's point.

tensions.dimension: the fundamental unit of information and the route to intelligence: meaningless bits processed by brute force (scaling channel capacity) vs. meaningful lists organized by modular abstraction
tensions.conditions_a: Shannon information better describes credit assignment when the problem is closed and IID — a stable distribution of possible messages (a fixed maze, next-word prediction within a known language) — so a linear increase in channel capacity exponentially improves signal-to-noise and brute force suffices.
tensions.conditions_b: Simon information better describes credit assignment when problems are novel/OOD and must be decomposed, where added channel capacity cannot substitute for better abstractions (lists) and meaning/designation is required to avoid processing every detail.

probes.prompt: Sutton's 'bitter lesson' says scaling compute (brute force) beats clever strategy; Simon's watchmaker says modular abstraction beats scale. When does just adding capacity win, and when does it fail? Use the IID vs OOD distinction in your answer.
expected_signals: Frames brute force as winning when the problem is closed/IID — a stable distribution of possible messages (e.g. a fixed game, next-word prediction in a known language).
Frames modularity/abstraction as winning when problems are novel/OOD and must be decomposed.
Connects bits-vs-lists (meaningless syntactic units vs meaningful designating units) to the two strategies.
Notes that adding channel capacity cannot substitute for better abstractions when meaning/designation is required.
Keeps it conditional — does not crown one approach universally correct.
